summary: Defines MIB objects for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units, the Ethernet interface hardware. It obsoletes RFC 3636 and changes how MAU type identities are handled.

eli5.summary: A medium attachment unit is the part of an Ethernet port that touches the cable. This lists the gauges a manager can read to see its type and state.

subtitle: The SNMP MIB for Ethernet's physical-layer attachment units, now split so new media types need no new RFC.

tldr.problem: Every time the IEEE 802.3 working group defined a new kind of Ethernet medium attachment unit, the MAU MIB had to be revised, and the earlier version, RFC 3636, did not cover Ethernet in the First Mile (EFM) or 10GBASE-CX4.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4836 keeps the managed objects in the MAU-MIB module and moves the MAU type identities and related textual conventions into a separate IANA-maintained module, IANA-MAU-MIB, which IANA can reissue when a new MAU appears.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3636 and adds EFM and 10GBASE-CX4 support, at the cost of not being entirely backward-compatible with MIB modules that imported MAU type identities from the MAU-MIB.

today: RFC 4836 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2007, and it obsoletes RFC 3636. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MAU MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4836 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs). Objects in the MIB are normally read and set through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are defined with the Structure of Management Information, version 2 (SMIv2), described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The definitions follow Section 30.5 (Layer Management for MAUs), Section 30.6 (Management for link Auto-Negotiation) and Annex 30A of IEEE Std. 802.3-2005. The stated goal is to manage all types of Ethernet/802.3 MAUs.

The RFC distinguishes two kinds of device for convenience. Repeater MAUs are connected to IEEE 802.3 repeaters, and interface MAUs are connected to 802.3 (Ethernet-like) interfaces.
sections.eli5: Think of a dashboard for one plug on a network box. The dashboard shows what kind of cable it expects and whether it is working.

sections.title: Relationship to RFC 3636
sections.content:
The definitions are intended to be a superset of those in RFC 3636, which RFC 4836 obsoletes. The previous document defined a single MIB module. This one splits it in two, putting frequently updated object identities and textual conventions into a separate, IANA-maintained module named IANA-MAU-MIB. That reduces the need to update the basic MAU-MIB module.

The new IANA module also adds definitions for Ethernet in the First Mile (EFM) and 10GBASE-CX4 interfaces, from IEEE Std 802.3ah-2004 and IEEE Std 802.3ak-2004.

The change is not entirely backward-compatible. MIB modules that import MAU type object identity descriptors from the MAU-MIB must be revised to import them from the IANA-MAU-MIB. The RFC admits this deviates from the SMIv2 revision rules but says the maintenance cost of not doing it justified the deviation, and that the working group found no examples of modules or applications that would actually be harmed.
sections.eli5: The list of cable types used to live inside the main book, so every new cable meant a new edition. Now the list is a separate loose-leaf binder that can be updated alone.

sections.title: How It Fits With Other MIBs
sections.content:
An agent implementing the MAU-MIB is assumed to implement at least the system group of the SNMPv2 MIB (RFC 3418).

The interface-MAU objects extend the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863). An agent that implements them MUST also implement the relevant groups of the ifCompliance3 statement and fully comply with dot3Compliance2 of the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB (RFC 3635). The value of ifMauIfIndex is the same as the ifIndex of the interface the MAU is connected to.

For 10GBASE-W PHYs, the agent MUST also support the Ethernet WAN Interface Sublayer (WIS) MIB (RFC 3637) and its interface layering model. If the MAU type can change dynamically, the agent creates or destroys the WIS-related table entries as ifMauDefaultType moves to or from a 10GBASE-W type.

The repeater-MAU objects extend the 802.3 Repeater MIB (RFC 2108), and an agent MUST comply with its snmpRptrModCompl statement. Repeater ports are not represented as interfaces in the Interface MIB.
sections.eli5: This dashboard plugs into other dashboards. Each plug on the box has a number, and the MAU gauges use the same number so everything lines up.

sections.title: Mapping IEEE 802.3 Objects to SNMP Objects
sections.content:
The MIB is built from the managed objects (attributes) of IEEE 802.3 Clause 30, and Table 1 of the RFC maps each to an SNMP object. For example, the MAU type attribute (aMAUType) maps to rpMauType or ifMauType, the media-available attribute maps to rpMauMediaAvailable or ifMauMediaAvailable, and the jabber attribute maps to the jabber state and jabbering-state-enter counters.

Auto-negotiation attributes map to ifMau objects such as ifMauAutoNegAdminStatus, ifMauAutoNegRestart and ifMauAutoNegCapabilityBits. Objects for broadband MAUs use the broadMau prefix.

A few IEEE objects are deliberately left out. aIdleErrorCount is only useful for 100BaseT2, which the RFC says is not widely implemented, and the selector-ability attributes are only needed for isoethernet (802.9a), which the MAU-MIB does not support.

A MAU can also be internal, implemented entirely within a device. If it is managed, its objects appear in dot3RpMauBasicGroup for repeater MAUs or dot3IfMauBasicGroup for interface MAUs.
sections.eli5: The official Ethernet rulebook lists things you can check on a plug. This section is the translation table from the rulebook's names to the names the network manager actually types.

sections.title: Adding New MAU Types
sections.content:
The dot3MauType object identifiers and their OBJECT-IDENTITY definitions moved from the MAU-MIB into IANA-MAU-MIB. When IEEE 802.3 defines a new MAU, IANA can reissue that module with the new identity and its matching bit in IANAifMauTypeListBits, and possibly new values for IANAifMauMediaAvailable, IANAifMauAutoNegCapBits or IANAifJackType.

The syntax of the type-list, media-available and auto-negotiation capability objects is now given by these textual conventions rather than by inline enumerations. The old JackType convention is deprecated in favour of IANAifJackType.

An Expert Review, as defined in RFC 2434, is REQUIRED to add a new MAU, media-available state, auto-negotiation capability or jack type. If a new MAU needs additional managed objects or changes how existing ones behave, a standards-track specification is also REQUIRED, and it must note side effects such as the ones for 10GBASE-W MAUs.
sections.eli5: When a new kind of cable is invented, only the cable list is updated, after an expert checks it. The main manual stays the same unless the new cable behaves in a truly new way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IANA-MAU-MIB defines only textual conventions, so the RFC says meaningful security considerations apply only to the MAU-MIB. Several of its objects are read-write, and setting them can seriously affect the network: enabling or disabling a MAU, changing its default type, enabling, disabling or restarting auto-negotiation, and changing the capabilities it advertises. Some readable objects may also be sensitive, since they expose statistics and status about individual links.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS implementors consider the SNMPv3 security features, with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions earlier than SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators remain responsible for configuring the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can read or change the objects.
sections.eli5: Some switches on the dashboard can turn a plug off. So only trusted people should be allowed to touch them, and their messages should be locked.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines the first version of the IANA-maintained IANA-MAU-MIB. Each new MAU type, media-available state, auto-negotiation capability or jack type that the IEEE 802.3 working group defines, and that is approved for publication in a revision of IEEE Std 802.3, is intended to be added to it, provided it can be managed by the base objects in the MAU-MIB.

For each new MAU type, a short description of the technology and, wherever possible, a reference to a publicly available specification SHOULD be given. An Expert Review is REQUIRED for each modification.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official cable list. Each new entry needs a short description and a check by an expert.
